claim: The Toll pathway was first identified as a master regulator of dorso-ventral patterning in the Drosophila embryo.
source: The Toll pathway was first identified as a master regulator of dorso-ventral patterning in the Drosophila embryo (Anderson et al., 1985)
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 1985

claim: The Toll pathway serves as the core mechanism for the innate immune response to Gram positive bacteria, fungi, viruses and cancer cells in both Drosophila and mammals.
source: The Toll pathway was first identified as a master regulator of dorso-ventral patterning in the Drosophila embryo (Anderson et al., 1985) and subsequently shown to serve as the core mechanism for the innate immune response to Gram positive bacteria, fungi, viruses and cancer cells in both Drosophila and mammals (Lemaitre et al., 1996; Medzhitov et al., 1997; Krutzik et al., 2001; Silverman and Maniatis, 2001; Thoma-Uszynski et al., 2001; Hoffmann and Reichhart, 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: In Drosophila the Toll pathway is activated upon infection via the proteolytic cleavage of the cytokine Spätzle.
source: In Drosophila the Toll pathway is activated upon infection via the proteolytic cleavage of the cytokine Spätzle (Chasan and Anderson, 1989; Weber et al., 2003; Stein et al., 1991)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of Spätzle triggers a signal transduction cascade that leads to the nuclear translocation of the NFκB transcription factors Dorsal and Dif.
source: In Drosophila the Toll pathway is activated upon infection via the proteolytic cleavage of the cytokine Spätzle (Chasan and Anderson, 1989; Weber et al., 2003; Stein et al., 1991), which triggers a signal transduction cascade that leads to the nuclear translocation of the NFκB transcription factors Dorsal and Dif (Drier et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Drier et al., 1999

claim: The Toll signaling cascade starts with the binding of cleaved Spätzle to one of the nine Toll receptors.
source: This ancient and highly conserved cascade starts with the binding of cleaved Spätzle to one of the nine Toll receptors
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the Toll pathway

claim: The Toll receptor associates via its cytoplasmic domain with Myd88, Tube and Pelle.
source: This ancient and highly conserved cascade starts with the binding of cleaved Spätzle to one of the nine Toll receptors, which in turn associates via its cytoplasmic domain with Myd88, Tube and Pelle.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the Toll pathway

claim: The kinase Pelle phosphorylates Cactus (IκB), targeting it for proteosomal degradation.
source: The kinase Pelle then phosphorylates Cactus (IκB), targeting it for proteosomal degradation (Horng and Medzhitov, 2001; Sun et al., 2002; Wu and Anderson, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Cactus normally retains Dorsal and Dif in the cytoplasm.
source: Since Cactus normally retains Dorsal and Dif in the cytoplasm, its degradation causes their release, nuclear translocation and expression of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), molecules that specifically fight infection (Bulet et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation support

claim: Degradation of Cactus causes the release and nuclear translocation of Dorsal and Dif and expression of antimicrobial peptides.
source: Since Cactus normally retains Dorsal and Dif in the cytoplasm, its degradation causes their release, nuclear translocation and expression of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), molecules that specifically fight infection (Bulet et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bulet et al., 1999

claim: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are molecules that specifically fight infection.
source: Since Cactus normally retains Dorsal and Dif in the cytoplasm, its degradation causes their release, nuclear translocation and expression of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), molecules that specifically fight infection (Bulet et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bulet et al., 1999

claim: The Toll pathway has been proposed to mediate the elimination of unfit cells via a process known as cell competition.
source: The Toll pathway has more recently been proposed to mediate the elimination of unfit cells (Meyer et al., 2014) from tissues via a process known in Drosophila and mammals as cell competition (Morata and Ripoll, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meyer et al., 2014 and Morata and Ripoll, 1975

claim: In cell competition, weakened or damaged 'loser' cells are detected and eliminated from developing tissues via delamination and apoptosis when surrounded by fitter 'winner' cells.
source: Weakened, damaged cells, referred to as 'losers' in the context of cell competition, are detected and eliminated from developing tissues via delamination and apoptosis when surrounded by fitter cells, generally referred to as 'winners'.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about cell competition

claim: Minute competition is a paradigm of cell competition where cells lacking one allele of a ribosomal protein gene are surrounded by wild-type cells.
source: Two well studied paradigms of cell competition are: Minute competition, where cells lacking one allele of a ribosomal protein gene are surrounded by wild-type cells (Morata and Ripoll, 1975)
evidence: Supported by citation to Morata and Ripoll, 1975

claim: Super-competition is a paradigm of cell competition where wild-type cells are surrounded by cells expressing elevated levels of Myc.
source: super-competition, where wild-type cells are surrounded by cells expressing elevated levels of Myc (Moreno and Basler, 2004; de la Cova et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Overexpression of Cactus in loser cells rescues cell competition-driven elimination of both RpL14+/- Minute clones and wild-type clones surrounded by cells with an extra copy of the dMyc gene.
source: Overexpression (OE) of Cactus in loser cells rescues cell competition-driven elimination of both RpL14+/-Minute clones and of wild-type clones surrounded by cells with an extra copy of the dMyc gene (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2014

claim: dMyc-expressing winner cells release Spätzle and the serine proteases required for its activation, thereby enhancing Toll-dependent apoptosis in neighboring loser cells.
source: It has recently been proposed that dMyc-expressing winner cells release Spätzle and the serine proteases required for its activation, thereby enhancing Toll-dependent apoptosis in neighboring loser cells (Alpar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alpar et al., 2018

claim: Inhibition of the Toll pathway by Cactus overexpression confers a clonal growth advantage to wild-type cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we observed that inhibition of the Toll pathway by Cactus OE not only rescued the elimination of loser cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but also conferred a clonal growth advantage to wild-type cells (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Activation of the Toll pathway via Toll-7 or Pelle overexpression causes a reduction of clonal growth.
source: Moreover, the activation of the pathway via Toll-7 or Pelle overexpression caused a reduction of clonal growth: such clones assumed a rounded-up shape, suggesting that cells were undergoing apoptosis (Figure 1A–1A''', quantified in 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-1A''' and quantified in 1B

claim: Toll-7 or Pelle overexpressing clones assume a rounded-up shape, suggesting that cells are undergoing apoptosis.
source: Moreover, the activation of the pathway via Toll-7 or Pelle overexpression caused a reduction of clonal growth: such clones assumed a rounded-up shape, suggesting that cells were undergoing apoptosis (Figure 1A–1A''', quantified in 1B).
evidence: Based on morphological observation in Figure 1A-1A''' and inference about apoptosis

claim: Overexpression of Dorsal, Tollo and Toll-2 leads to a reduction of clonal growth.
source: Additional regimes of clonal induction (Figure 1C–D) and the use of other pathway components (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3) corroborated these results: also overexpression of Dorsal, Tollo and Toll-2 led to a reduction of clonal growth
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3

claim: Overexpression of Toll-10b, the constitutive active form of the Toll-1 receptor, leads to a reduction of clonal growth.
source: as well as the overexpression of Toll-10b, the constitutive active form of the Toll-1 receptor.
evidence: Stated as experimental result in the context of other pathway components

claim: Both Toll-7 and Pelle overexpressing clones are highly apoptotic.
source: Dcp-1 staining revealed that both Toll-7 and Pelle OE clones are highly apoptotic, round up and are finally pushed out of the tissue via delamination (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by Dcp-1 staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Toll-7 and Pelle overexpressing clones round up and are finally pushed out of the tissue via delamination.
source: Dcp-1 staining revealed that both Toll-7 and Pelle OE clones are highly apoptotic, round up and are finally pushed out of the tissue via delamination (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Toll-7 overexpression in the posterior compartment of the wing disc massively induces apoptosis compared to the wild-type anterior compartment.
source: Toll-7 OE massively induced apoptosis, whereas Cactus OE caused a reduction of apoptosis when compared to the wild-type anterior compartment (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: Cactus overexpression in the posterior compartment of the wing disc causes a reduction of apoptosis compared to the wild-type anterior compartment.
source: Toll-7 OE massively induced apoptosis, whereas Cactus OE caused a reduction of apoptosis when compared to the wild-type anterior compartment (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: The Toll pathway does not regulate growth systemically, as no major size differences could be observed in entire animals or whole appendages with altered pathway activity.
source: In order to determine whether the Toll pathway regulates growth systemically, we analyzed entire animals or whole appendages with altered pathway activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 6). However, no major size differences could be observed
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6

claim: Toll signaling influences cellular fitness only in situations where cell populations that differ in their ability to respond to infection are intermingled.
source: However, no major size differences could be observed, indicating that Toll signaling influences cellular fitness only in situations where cell populations that differ in their ability to respond to infection are intermingled.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that systemic changes do not affect size

claim: Wild-type cells must exhibit higher Toll pathway activity compared to Cactus overexpressing cells.
source: A corollary of this hypothesis would be that wild-type cells must exhibit higher pathway activity compared to Cactus OE cells, in which the pathway is effectively blocked.
evidence: Inferred from the hypothesis about intermingled cell populations

claim: A subliminal Toll pathway activity level may stem from chronic exposure to pathogens due to typically unsterile working conditions.
source: Since Toll signaling is a key mediator for the immune response, it is possible that a subliminal pathway activity level stems from chronic exposure to pathogens, due to typically unsterile working conditions.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the source of pathway activity

claim: Aspergillus niger was chosen for infection experiments because of its pathogenic activity that shortens the life span of flies.
source: This fungus was chosen because of its pathogenic activity that shortens the life span of flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: In a Minute cell competition scenario, the inhibition of the Toll pathway via overexpression of Cactus in loser cells strongly rescues their elimination in both normal and infected conditions.
source: As expected, in a Minute cell competition scenario, the inhibition of the Toll pathway via overexpression of Cactus in loser cells strongly rescued their elimination in both normal and infected conditions (Figure 2A'–A'', B'–B'', quantified in Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A'-A'', B'-B'', quantified in Figure 2E, F

claim: No rescue of cell competition-driven elimination of loser cells is observed when animals are grown under axenic conditions.
source: However, no rescue of cell competition-driven elimination of loser cells was observed when animals were grown under axenic conditions (Figure 2A,B, quantified in Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B, quantified in Figure 2E, F

claim: Under axenic conditions Cactus overexpressing Minute loser clones are eliminated even more efficiently than control Minute clones.
source: Indeed, under axenic conditions Cactus OE Minute loser clones were eliminated even more efficiently than control Minute clones (Figure 2A,B,C–D', quantified in Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B, C-D', quantified in Figure 2E, F

claim: In the dMyc super-competition context, Cactus overexpression rescues loser cell elimination upon infection but not under axenic conditions.
source: A similar behavior was observed in the dMyc super-competition context, where Cactus OE rescued loser cell elimination upon infection but not under axenic conditions (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: The involvement of the Toll pathway in cell competition depends on the presence of pathogens in the environment in which larvae develop.
source: Thus the involvement of the Toll pathway in cell competition depends on the presence of pathogens in the environment in which larvae develop.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects observed under axenic, normal, and infected conditions

claim: Under extra-pathogen conditions Cactus-dependent overgrowth is further enhanced.
source: The clonal growth influence by Cactus OE in wild-type cells also depends on the state of infection. Under extra-pathogen conditions Cactus-dependent overgrowth was further enhanced, but suppressed under axenic conditions (Figure 3A–B'', quantified in Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B'', quantified in Figure 3D

claim: Under axenic conditions Cactus-dependent overgrowth is suppressed.
source: The clonal growth influence by Cactus OE in wild-type cells also depends on the state of infection. Under extra-pathogen conditions Cactus-dependent overgrowth was further enhanced, but suppressed under axenic conditions (Figure 3A–B'', quantified in Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B'', quantified in Figure 3D

claim: Clones overexpressing Toll-7 are rare and small in both normal and axenic conditions.
source: The opposite effect could be observed when clones overexpress Toll-7: clones were rare and small in both normal and axenic conditions, but grew almost as well as control LacZ clones upon highly infected conditions (Figure 3C–C'', quantified in Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-C'', quantified in Figure 3D

claim: Clones overexpressing Toll-7 grow almost as well as control LacZ clones upon highly infected conditions.
source: The opposite effect could be observed when clones overexpress Toll-7: clones were rare and small in both normal and axenic conditions, but grew almost as well as control LacZ clones upon highly infected conditions (Figure 3C–C'', quantified in Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-C'', quantified in Figure 3D

claim: The clonal disadvantage caused by Toll pathway activation inversely correlates with the level of infection, substantially diminishing with increasing degrees of infection.
source: Thus the clonal disadvantage caused by Toll pathway activation inversely correlates with the level of infection, substantially diminishing with increasing degrees of infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Toll-7 overexpressing clones grow better under infected conditions

claim: Pathway activation-induced lethality is ameliorated under conditions of extra-infection.
source: We found that pathway activation-induced lethality was ameliorated under conditions of extra-infection, while pathway suppression-induced lethality was rescued by axenic conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Pathway suppression-induced lethality is rescued by axenic conditions.
source: We found that pathway activation-induced lethality was ameliorated under conditions of extra-infection, while pathway suppression-induced lethality was rescued by axenic conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: In a non-sterile environment cells deficient for the Toll-mediated immune response grow better than immunocompetent wild-type cells.
source: In conclusion, our findings reveal that in a non-sterile environment cells deficient for the Toll-mediated immune response grow better than immunocompetent wild-type cells.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing Cactus OE clones grow better under normal and infected conditions

claim: The growth difference between Toll-deficient and immunocompetent cells depends on the level of infection: it is null in axenic conditions and enhanced by addition of pathogens.
source: This growth difference depends on the level of infection: it is null in axenic conditions and enhanced by addition of pathogens.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results across different infection conditions

claim: The growth difference driven by different levels of Toll pathway activity must occur in cell populations that cohabitate in the same tissue.
source: Most likely, therefore, it is driven by different levels of Toll pathway activity. Importantly though, these different levels must occur in cell populations that cohabitate in the same tissue, as we were not able to detect growth effects in organs entirely programmed to exhibit elevated or reduced Toll signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that systemic changes do not affect growth

claim: Cells with lower Toll pathway activity profit from, and grow faster than, nearby cells with higher activity.
source: Our findings can therefore be explained by a model (Figure 4) in which cells with lower Toll pathway activity profit from, and grow faster than, nearby cells with higher activity.
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental findings

claim: Cell clones with higher Toll signaling levels are eliminated from the tissue via apoptosis and delamination when surrounded by cells with lower levels.
source: Conversely, cell clones with higher Toll signaling levels (e.g. by overexpressing Toll receptors) are eliminated from the tissue via apoptosis and delamination when surrounded by cells with lower levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental findings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The local effects on clonal growth depend on a systemic response to infection.
source: Our experiments indirectly suggest that the local effects on clonal growth depend on a systemic response to infection.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: The active form of Spätzle is likely produced in distant organs and reaches the wing disc through the haemolymph.
source: Likely therefore, the active form of Spätzle is produced in distant organs and reaches the wing disc through the haemolymph.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the systemic response hypothesis

claim: Wing discs locally produce Spätzle and the serine proteases responsible for its activation.
source: However, it has recently been proposed that wing discs locally produce Spätzle and the serine proteases responsible for its activation (Alpar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alpar et al., 2018

claim: Myc overexpressing cells may be able to induce Toll-dependent apoptosis in neighboring loser cells via an increased secretion of Spätzle and serine proteases.
source: Via an increased secretion of these factors, Myc OE cells may be able to induce Toll-dependent apoptosis in neighboring loser cells (Alpar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alpar et al., 2018

claim: Local and systemic sources of Spätzle may co-exist.
source: It is therefore possible that local and systemic sources of Spätzle co-exist.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the evidence for both local and systemic sources

claim: Dorsal induces the transcription of the pro-apoptotic gene rpr.
source: The previous findings that Dorsal induces the transcription of the pro-apoptotic gene rpr (Meyer et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2014

claim: The Drosophila Toll pathway cross-talks with the growth controlling Hippo signaling pathway.
source: and that the Drosophila Toll pathway cross-talks with the growth controlling Hippo signaling pathway (Liu et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016

claim: Life history theory seeks to explain natural selection on the basic assumption that environmental resources are limited and organisms establish trade-offs between processes such as reproduction, growth and immunity.
source: The evolutionary implications can be viewed in the light of the life history theory, which seeks to explain natural selection on the basic assumption that environmental resources are limited and organisms establish trade-offs between processes such as reproduction, growth and immunity (Roff, 1993; Stearns et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roff, 1993 and Stearns et al., 2000

claim: Allocating resources into immunity occurs at the expense of other important processes, such as organismal growth.
source: Allocating resources into a costly trait like immunity (van der Most et al., 2011; Rauw, 2012) occurs at the expense of other important processes, such as organismal growth.
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Most et al., 2011 and Rauw, 2012

claim: A cellular trade-off exists between innate immunity and clonal growth during development.
source: In agreement with this theory, we experimentally show that a cellular trade-off exists between innate immunity and clonal growth during development.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing growth differences based on Toll pathway activity

claim: Inhibition of the Toll pathway not only increases the fitness of loser cells, but also bestows a clonal growth advantage on wild-type cells.
source: In this work, we provide evidence that the inhibition of Toll signaling not only increases the fitness of loser cells, but also bestows a clonal growth advantage on wild-type cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The growth advantage conferred by Toll pathway inhibition depends on basal infection levels since it is no longer present under axenic conditions but exacerbated upon intense pathogen exposure.
source: We further demonstrate that this growth advantage depends on basal infection levels since it is no longer present under axenic conditions but exacerbated upon intense pathogen exposure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing axenic, normal, and infected conditions

claim: The Toll pathway functions as a fine-tuned pro-apoptotic and anti-proliferative regulator.
source: Thus, the Toll pathway functions as a fine-tuned pro-apoptotic and anti-proliferative regulator, underlining the existence of a trade-off between innate immunity and growth during development.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing apoptosis and growth effects

claim: There exists a trade-off between innate immunity and growth during development.
source: Thus, the Toll pathway functions as a fine-tuned pro-apoptotic and anti-proliferative regulator, underlining the existence of a trade-off between innate immunity and growth during development.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing growth differences based on Toll pathway activity and infection levels
